description: A middle-school earth science course built from the U.S. Geological Survey's classic free booklets for the public. Your child travels from the Earth's core through deep time, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, rocks and gems, and the world's deserts. Each day is a short USGS reading online plus a hands-on model, a map task, or a notebook sketch, with a few questions to talk over. Every booklet is a U.S. Government work in the public domain and free to read at pubs.usgs.gov.
includes: Link to the exact USGS booklet chapter for every lesson
Kitchen-table models: convection, seafloor spreading, faults, calderas, dunes
Questions with answers for every lesson

units.title: Unit 1: Inside the Earth and Deep Time

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The Earth's Crust
steps: Read the Introduction and The Crust in The Interior of the Earth
Draw the Earth as three shells (crust, mantle, core) and label how much of Earth's volume each takes up
Compare: how thick is oceanic crust under Hawaii versus continental crust under the Sierra Nevada?

links.label: Read The Interior of the Earth

questions: What percent of Earth's volume is the crust? The mantle? The core?
What did Isaac Newton figure out about the inside of the Earth?
answers: About 1 percent; about 84 percent; about 15 percent
Earth's average density is about twice that of surface rocks, so the inside must be made of denser material

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The Mantle, the Core, and the Moon
steps: Read The Mantle, The Core, and The Structure of the Moon
Trace the earthquake-wave paths in Figure 2 with a finger and find where S waves stop
Add the low-velocity zone, outer core, and inner core to yesterday's drawing

links.label: Read The Interior of the Earth

questions: How do scientists know the outer core is liquid?
Who discovered the core, and in what year?
answers: Shear (S) waves do not pass through it and P waves slow down sharply
R. D. Oldham, in 1906

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Putting Events in Order
steps: Read Introduction and Putting Events in Order in Fossils, Rocks, and Time
Put the six historical events from the booklet in order without using any dates, then check
Stack five books or towels and explain which was put down first and why
questions: In a pile of rock layers that has not been disturbed, which layer is oldest?
Why can we order events even without knowing their dates?
answers: The bottom layer
Because words like before and after, or layers lying on top of one another, show what came first

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Rocks and Layers
steps: Read Rocks and Layers
Make a table: gravel, sand, mud and what rock each one becomes
Shake soil, sand and pebbles in a jar of water, let it settle overnight, and sketch the layers
questions: What rock does sand become? What does mud become?
Why are most rocks at Earth's surface sedimentary rocks good 'pages' for reading Earth's history?
answers: Sandstone; mudstone or shale
They are laid down layer by layer and can bury and preserve living things, recording past events in order

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Fossils and Fossil Succession
steps: Read Fossils and Rocks and Fossil Succession
Write the three key ideas about fossils in your own words
Draw a column of rock layers and mark where you would stop finding flowering plants, birds and mammals as you go deeper
questions: Are most fossils from species that are still alive today?
Why do rocks of different ages hold different kinds of fossils?
About when did the last dinosaurs die out?
answers: No, most are from extinct species
Because life on Earth has changed through time
About 65 million years ago

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The Relative Time Scale
steps: Read The Relative Time Scale, and the Relative Time Scale page in Geologic Time
Look up what paleo-, meso-, ceno- and -zoic mean and name the three eras
Make a paper-strip time line of eons, eras and periods (oldest at the bottom)
questions: List the time divisions from largest to smallest.
What does 'Paleozoic' mean?
answers: Eons, eras, periods, epochs
Ancient animal life

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Numbers on the Time Scale: How Old Is the Earth?
steps: Read The Numeric Time Scale, then Radiometric Time Scale and Age of the Earth in Geologic Time
Explain radioactive decay with a 'half-life' game: start with 32 coins, shake, and remove the tails each round
Add numbers in millions of years to your paper time line

links.label: Geologic Time: Age of the Earth

questions: About how old is the Earth?
Why can't scientists date the Earth directly from its oldest rocks?
Besides Earth rocks, what else do scientists date to find Earth's age?
answers: About 4.5 to 4.6 billion years
Earth's first rocks have been recycled and destroyed by plate tectonics
Moon rocks and meteorites

lessons.title: Lesson 8: What Is Plate Tectonics?
steps: Read the Preface and the first part of Historical perspective (through Hutton's principle)
Read the side pages Inside the Earth and What is a tectonic plate?
Explain 'the present is the key to the past' with an everyday example
questions: What does the Greek root of 'tectonics' mean?
What does the name Pangaea mean?
Which idea replaced 'catastrophism' in the 1800s?
answers: To build
All lands
Uniformitarianism

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Wegener and Continental Drift
steps: Finish Historical perspective and read the Alfred Lothar Wegener side page
Cut out South America and Africa from a printed world map and fit them together
List Wegener's evidence and the one big question he could not answer
questions: What did fossils of tropical plants in Antarctica suggest to Wegener?
What was the fatal weakness in Wegener's theory?
answers: Antarctica was once closer to the equator, in a warmer climate
He could not explain what force could move the continents

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Mapping the Ocean Floor
steps: Read Developing the theory through 'Ocean floor mapping' and the mid-ocean ridge
Read the side page Exploring the deep ocean floor
Echo-sounding model: time a ball dropped into a tall box and explain how a 'ping' measures depth

links.label: Mid-ocean ridge, like a baseball seam

questions: What did the 1947 Atlantis survey find surprising about ocean-floor sediment?
How long is the global mid-ocean ridge?
answers: It was much thinner than expected
More than 50,000 kilometers

lessons.title: Lesson 11: Magnetic Stripes and Seafloor Spreading
steps: Read the magnetic striping and seafloor spreading sections of Developing the theory
Read the side pages Magnetic stripes and isotopic clocks and Harry Hammond Hess
Model it: pull two sheets of paper out of a slot between two desks, coloring a new stripe each time the 'field flips'
questions: What magnetic mineral in basalt records the Earth's field?
Where on the ocean floor are the youngest rocks?
Which ship's drill cores in 1968 gave the clinching evidence for seafloor spreading?
answers: Magnetite
At the crest of the mid-ocean ridge
The Glomar Challenger

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Divergent Boundaries
steps: Read the start of Understanding plate motions and the Divergent boundaries section
Find Iceland, the Red Sea, and the East African Rift on a map
Calculate: at 2.5 cm a year, how far does the Atlantic widen in your lifetime so far?
questions: Name the four kinds of plate boundaries.
Which country sits right on top of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
What might happen to the Horn of Africa if spreading continues?
answers: Divergent, convergent, transform, and plate-boundary zones
Iceland
It could become a large island

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Convergent Boundaries
steps: Read the Convergent boundaries sections (oceanic-continental, oceanic-oceanic, continental-continental)
Read the side pages Ring of Fire and The Himalayas
Push two towels together on a table to model a mountain range, then slide a stiff folder under a towel to model subduction
questions: What is a subduction zone?
Which mountains are rising where the Nazca Plate dives under South America?
Why must crust be destroyed somewhere if new crust is always forming?
answers: A place where one plate sinks under another
The Andes
Because the Earth is not getting bigger

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Transform Boundaries and How Fast Plates Move
steps: Read Transform boundaries, Plate-boundary zones, and Rates of motion
Read the side pages San Andreas fault and GPS satellite & receiver
Make a bar graph of the slowest and fastest spreading rates given in the text
questions: Who first described transform faults?
Which ridge spreads slowest, and which spreads fastest?
answers: J. Tuzo Wilson
The Arctic Ridge is slowest; the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island is fastest

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Hotspots
steps: Read "Hotspots": Mantle thermal plumes and the J. Tuzo Wilson side page
Hotspot model: slide a sheet of paper slowly over a fixed marker dot, tapping it down every few seconds
Find Yellowstone, Iceland and the Galapagos on the hotspot map

links.label: Prominent hotspots on a world map

questions: Why are the Hawaiian Islands older toward the northwest?
How does the legend of Pele match the geology?
answers: The Pacific Plate moves northwest over the hotspot, carrying older volcanoes away
Pele moved from Kauai southeast to Hawaii, the same direction the islands get younger
lessons.notes: The booklet's 1996 authors' note says newer studies question whether hotspots are deep and fixed; talk about how science keeps testing ideas.

lessons.title: Lesson 16: Some Unanswered Questions
steps: Read Some unanswered questions
Watch convection: heat water with a few drops of food coloring or rice grains and sketch the flow
Write a short paragraph: 'ridge push' or 'slab pull' — which do most scientists now favor, and why?
questions: What are the two main sources of heat inside the Earth?
Why have the Moon and Mars stopped being volcanically active?
answers: Radioactive decay and residual heat from Earth's formation
They are small, so they lost their internal heat faster

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Plate Tectonics and People
steps: Read Plate tectonics and people
Bend a thin stick until it snaps to model a locked fault releasing energy
Make a two-column chart of plate-tectonic hazards and natural resources

links.label: Tsunamis and the Ring of Fire

questions: Will California fall into the ocean in a big earthquake? Why or why not?
What is the difference between an earthquake's focus and its epicenter?
answers: No. The fault is only about 15 km deep and California's light continental crust rides high
The focus is the rupture point underground; the epicenter is the spot on the surface directly above it

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Earthquakes in History
steps: Read Introduction and Earthquakes in History in the booklet Earthquakes
Make a time line from the Chinese earthquake of 1177 B.C. to the 1906 San Francisco earthquake
Find New Madrid, Missouri, on a map and mark Boston and Denver, where its shaking was felt
questions: What is an earthquake, in one sentence?
Why did the huge 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes cause little loss of life?
answers: A sudden movement of the Earth caused by the release of strain that built up over a long time
The area was sparsely populated then

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Where Earthquakes Occur
steps: Read Where Earthquakes Occur
On a world map, color the three kinds of plate boundaries the booklet names
Compare this list with the four boundary types from This Dynamic Earth
questions: Where do most earthquakes happen?
Name the three kinds of plate boundaries described in this chapter.
answers: At the boundaries where plates meet
Spreading zones, transform faults, and subduction zones

lessons.title: Lesson 20: How Earthquakes Happen
steps: Read How Earthquakes Happen
Act out normal, reverse (thrust) and strike-slip faults with two blocks of wood or books
Draw a fault and label the focus and epicenter
questions: Besides moving crust, what else can cause an earthquake?
What happens to rock just before it 'snaps' to a new position?
answers: A volcanic eruption or a man-made explosion
It bends under stress until the stress exceeds the rock's strength

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Seismic Waves
steps: Read the first half of Measuring Earthquakes (seismographs and seismic waves)
Model P waves with a stretched Slinky pushed end-on, and S waves by shaking it side to side
Retell the order of waves felt at Valdez, Alaska, in 1964
questions: Which waves arrive first, and why are they called 'P' waves?
Which kind of body wave cannot pass through the Earth's molten core?
Which waves usually do the most damage?
answers: Compressional waves; they are primary, the fastest to arrive
Shear (S) waves
Surface waves

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Magnitude and Intensity
steps: Finish Measuring Earthquakes, then read Magnitude and Intensity in The San Andreas Fault
Work out: how many times more energy does a magnitude 8 release than a magnitude 6?
Write one sentence telling magnitude and intensity apart
questions: Ground motion of a magnitude 7 is how many times that of a magnitude 6?
Which scale describes how strongly shaking was felt at a place?
What is the smallest magnitude people normally feel?
answers: 10 times
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale
About magnitude 2

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Volcanoes, Prediction, and Probability
steps: Read Volcanoes and Earthquakes and Predicting Earthquakes
Work the booklet's example: four big quakes in 200 years means what chance in the next 50 years?
Discuss why 'random' timing might not be true on a real fault
questions: What do swarms of small earthquakes under a volcano tell scientists?
What two kinds of evidence do scientists use to estimate earthquake chances?
answers: That magma is moving inside the volcano
The history of large earthquakes in the area and the rate strain builds up in the rock
lessons.notes: This booklet was last reprinted in 1995; the USGS Earthquake Hazards Program site has current science.

lessons.title: Lesson 24: The San Andreas Fault: What and Where
steps: Read sections I to III of The San Andreas Fault
Trace the fault on a map of California from the Gulf of California to Cape Mendocino
Label the Pacific Plate and North American Plate with arrows showing how they move
questions: Which two plates meet along the San Andreas fault?
How long is the whole San Andreas fault system?
answers: The Pacific Plate and the North American Plate
More than 800 miles

lessons.title: Lesson 25: Reading the Landscape Along a Fault
steps: Read sections V and VI (surface features and movement)
Draw a stream crossing the fault before and after it is offset to the right
Find Crystal Springs Reservoir or Tomales Bay on an online map and look for the straight fault valley
questions: What is 'right-lateral strike-slip' movement?
What was the largest offset measured in the 1906 earthquake, and where?
answers: Blocks slide sideways so the far side appears to move to the right
Almost 21 feet, on the road across the head of Tomales Bay

lessons.title: Lesson 26: Living with Earthquakes
steps: Read sections VII to XI (what is an earthquake through what can be done)
List the three lines of defense against earthquake hazards
Make a family earthquake plan: a safe spot in each room and a meeting place outside

links.label: Read VII. What Is an Earthquake?
Read IX. Earthquakes Along the Fault
Read X. When Could the Next Large Earthquake Occur
Read XI. What Can Be Done

questions: What is a 'seismic gap'?
About how often have large earthquakes struck the southern San Andreas fault?
answers: A fault segment with no large earthquake for a long time
About every 150 years

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Volcanoes Destroy and Create
steps: Read the Introduction and The Nature of Volcanoes in the booklet Volcanoes
Make a list of three things volcanoes destroy and three things they create
Draw a volcano and label vent, magma reservoir, lava, and tephra
questions: About how much of Earth's surface is of volcanic origin?
How are volcanoes different from other mountains?
answers: More than 80 percent
They are built up from their own erupted material, not by folding or uplift

lessons.title: Lesson 28: Four Kinds of Volcanoes
steps: Read Principal Types of Volcanoes
Build cinder-cone, shield and composite models out of play dough or damp sand and compare slopes
Make a chart: type, shape, what it is built of, one example
questions: What are the four main kinds of volcanoes?
What grew in a Mexican cornfield starting in 1943?
What is another name for a composite volcano?
answers: Cinder cones, composite volcanoes, shield volcanoes, and lava domes
Parícutin, a cinder cone
Stratovolcano

lessons.title: Lesson 29: Plugs, Maars, and Undersea Volcanoes
steps: Read Other Volcanic Structures and Submarine Volcanoes
Look up a photo of Ship Rock, New Mexico, as an example of a volcanic neck
Explain in your own words why deep-sea eruptions may not disturb the ocean surface
questions: What is a volcanic plug or neck?
How are black-sand beaches made?
answers: Hardened magma left in a volcano's feeding pipe after the cone erodes
Lava meeting the sea cools so fast it shatters into sand and rubble

lessons.title: Lesson 30: Types of Eruptions
steps: Read Types of Volcanic Eruptions
Make a scale from gentle to violent and place Hawaiian, Strombolian, Vulcanian, Vesuvian and Peléan eruptions on it
Shake a soda bottle and open it over a sink to talk about gas pressure (carefully!)
questions: What is a nuée ardente?
Which kind of eruption destroyed St. Pierre on Martinique in 1902?
answers: A glowing avalanche of hot gas, ash and lava fragments rushing downslope
A Peléan eruption of Mont Pelée

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Geysers, Fumaroles, and Hot Springs
steps: Read Geysers, Fumaroles, and Hot Springs
Draw the underground path water takes to become a geyser
Look up the current eruption interval of Old Faithful

links.label: Read Geysers, Fumaroles, and Hot Springs

questions: Why are these features sometimes called 'dying volcanoes'?
What makes a geyser suddenly erupt?
answers: They seem to be the last stage of activity as magma below cools
Some of the heated water suddenly flashes into steam and blasts the water out

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Volcanoes, Plates, and Other Worlds
steps: Read Plate-Tectonics Theory and Extraterrestrial Volcanism
Mark plate-boundary volcanoes and intra-plate volcanoes on a world map in two colors
Compare a picture of Olympus Mons on Mars with Mauna Loa
questions: What is an 'intra-plate' volcano? Give an example.
What kind of volcano do Martian and Hawaiian volcanoes both resemble?
answers: A volcano far from a plate boundary, such as the Hawaiian Islands
Shield volcanoes

lessons.title: Lesson 33: Watching Volcanoes
steps: Read Volcano Monitoring and Research and Volcanoes and People
List the tools scientists use to watch a restless volcano
Debate: why do people live on the slopes of volcanoes?
questions: Whose letters about Vesuvius in A.D. 79 are often called the start of volcanology?
Name two ways volcanoes help people.
answers: Pliny the Younger
Any two: fertile soils, building materials, abrasives and industrial materials, geothermal energy

lessons.title: Lesson 34: Volcanoes of the United States: Hawaii and the Cascades
steps: Read the Introduction, Volcanoes and the Theory of Plate Tectonics, and the Hawaiian and Cascade sections of Volcanoes of the United States
Find Kilauea, Mauna Loa, Mount St. Helens, Mount Rainier and Mount Shasta on a U.S. map
Compare the eruptions of Kilauea and Mount St. Helens in a Venn diagram

links.label: Read Volcanoes and the Theory of Plate Tectonics

questions: Why are Cascade volcanoes more dangerous than Kilauea?
In what year did Mount St. Helens erupt so destructively?
answers: They erupt violently and explosively and sit near populated, farmed areas

lessons.title: Lesson 35: Alaska, Calderas, and Ancient Volcanoes
steps: Read the Alaskan volcanoes, Restless calderas, and Active Volcanoes: Windows into the Past sections
Model a caldera: bury a balloon under flour, let some air out, and watch the surface sink
Look for volcanic rock (basalt, pumice, obsidian) in your own area or a rock shop

links.label: Read Active Volcanoes: Windows into the Past

questions: What is a caldera and how does it form?
Which 1912 Alaskan eruption is the most recent caldera-forming eruption there?
answers: A huge depression formed when the ground collapses after a large volume of magma is erupted
Novarupta, in Katmai

lessons.title: Lesson 36: Rocks Tell the Story of the Earth
steps: Read Rocks Tell the Story of the Earth and Types of Rocks in Collecting Rocks
Sort a handful of rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic as best you can
Draw the rock cycle with arrows between the three groups
questions: What are the three groups of rocks?
Why does slowly cooled magma make coarse-grained rock?
answers: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic
Crystals have time to grow large when magma cools slowly deep underground

lessons.title: Lesson 37: Starting a Rock Collection
steps: Read Starting a Collection through Hints for Rock Collectors
Gather equipment (bags, marker, notebook, hand lens) and go on a short collecting walk
Label each specimen with where and when you found it
questions: Why should you write down where each rock was found?
What kind of map helps you find and identify rocks in an area?
answers: A specimen is much more useful when you know its source, so you can match it with geologic maps and other collections
A geologic map
lessons.notes: Collect only where it is allowed; many parks forbid taking rocks.

lessons.title: Lesson 38: What Makes a Gemstone?
steps: Read Key Terminology and Geologic Environment in Natural Gemstones
Write the difference between a gemstone, a gem, and a mineral
List the three qualities of a precious gemstone
questions: What three qualities does a precious gemstone have?
Why are gemstones usually hard to find?
answers: Beauty, durability, and rarity
They are scattered sparsely through rock rather than in big deposits

lessons.title: Lesson 39: Hardness, Weight, and Organic Gems
steps: Read Mineral Gemstones and Organic Gemstones
Do a scratch test: fingernail, copper coin, steel nail, and glass on several rocks; rank them on the Mohs scale
Pick one organic gemstone and explain where it comes from
questions: What is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale, and what is the softest?
What is amber?
What does specific gravity compare?
answers: Diamond (10); talc (1)
Hardened fossil resin or sap of ancient trees
How heavy a gemstone is compared with the same volume of water

lessons.title: Lesson 40: What Is a Desert?
steps: Read What Is a Desert? and How the Atmosphere Influences Aridity in Deserts: Geology and Resources
On a globe, find the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn
Sketch how air rises at the Equator and sinks around 30 degrees latitude

links.label: Read How the Atmosphere Influences Aridity

questions: About how much of Earth's land is desert?
Do all deserts have to be hot?
answers: About one-third
No; they are defined by dryness and can be cold

lessons.title: Lesson 41: Where Deserts Form and Kinds of Deserts
steps: Read Where Deserts Form and Types of Deserts
Make a chart of the six desert types with one example of each
Model a rain shadow: blow a fine mist over a book 'mountain' and see which side stays dry
questions: What is the world's largest (hot) desert?
What is a paleodesert?
answers: The Sahara
A former desert area that is no longer arid

lessons.title: Lesson 42: Desert Features and the Work of Wind
steps: Read Desert Features and Eolian Processes
Use a hair dryer on a tray of mixed sand and gravel and watch deflation leave the pebbles behind
Define deflation and abrasion in your notebook
questions: About how much of the world's desert surface is covered by sand?
What does 'eolian' refer to?
answers: Only about 20 percent
The activity of the wind

lessons.title: Lesson 43: Dunes and Seeing Deserts from Space
steps: Read Types of Dunes and Remote Sensing of Arid Lands
Sketch the five basic dune shapes and show the wind direction for crescentic dunes
Look at a satellite map of a desert and find a dune field

links.label: Read Remote Sensing of Arid Lands

questions: Name the five basic types of dunes.
What is the most common dune form on Earth and Mars?
What is remote sensing?
answers: Crescentic, linear, star, dome, and parabolic
Crescentic
Collecting information about something without touching it, such as with satellite images

lessons.title: Lesson 44: Desert Riches and Desertification
steps: Read Mineral Resources in Deserts and Desertification
Evaporate salt water in a shallow dish in the sun to see how evaporites form
Write a short paragraph on one way people can slow desertification
questions: How does evaporation help make mineral deposits in deserts?
What drought beginning in 1968 caused great loss of life in Africa?
answers: Water evaporates from desert lakes and leaves dissolved minerals behind
The Sahelian drought
